summary.text: An 11-year-old girl from a rural community was referred to a pediatric dentistry clinic for comprehensive dental care. A previous hematologist had diagnosed symptomatic mild hemophilia A with 46% factor VIII activity and normal von Willebrand factor; she was under on-demand treatment and her father had moderate hemophilia A. A previous extraction by a general dentist had caused excessive, uncontrolled bleeding.

At the first visit she had a comprehensive assessment with examinations, charting, clinical photographs and radiographs. A phased plan coordinated with Hematology specified factor VIII coverage for invasive procedures, infiltration anesthesia, meticulous local hemostasis and analgesia avoiding NSAIDs.

At the second visit she received 1,000 IU of factor VIII one hour before the appointment, then extractions of #55, #53, #65, #75 and a mesiodens under topical benzocaine for mobile primary teeth and limited lidocaine with epinephrine infiltration for #65 and the mesiodens, with hemostasis by sterile gauze. She was observed for 30 minutes and discharged with written instructions to avoid NSAIDs and use acetaminophen; no postoperative bleeding or complications occurred. Postoperative photographs were taken at 30 minutes and one month.

Subsequent restorative and preventive visits proceeded without factor coverage: resin restorations of #21, #36 and #12, and sealants of #46, #16 and #26, with rubber-dam or relative isolation and no dental clamp. Additional visits covered hygiene reinforcement, prophylaxis and fluoride varnish.

Hematology advised factor replacement around menarche and encouraged follow-up, the wording differing between prophylactic and on-demand. She was referred to orthodontics for malocclusion, and there were no bleeding events related to dental care throughout follow-up.
